Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(3))^{3} & ={([\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(2) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{2}(3)\end{aligned}])}^{3} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}({J}_{2}(2))^{3} & 0 \\ 0 & ({J}_{2}(3))^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =({J}_{2}(2))^{3}\,⊕\,({J}_{2}(3))^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{2}(2),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =2.$ Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(2)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{2}^{3} & 3\cdot {2}^{2} \\ 0 & {2}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 12 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{2}(3),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =3.$ Since $n=2,$ we need the first derivative of $f$ only, which we have already computed. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(3)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(3) & {f}^{′}(3) \\ 0 & f(3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{3} & 3\cdot {3}^{2} \\ 0 & {3}^{3}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}27 & 27 \\ 0 & 27\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(3))^{3}=({J}_{2}(2))^{3}\,⊕\,({J}_{2}(3))^{3}=[\begin{aligned}8 & 12 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 27 & 27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 27\end{aligned}].
$$
